title: Frugality & Extensibility
summary: Frugality is cost per unit of useful work at SLO; extensibility is cost of the next change. Design budgets for the first and seams for the second.

Understanding Frugality: What It Means to Live Simply

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: A frugal system knows its **cost per 1k useful requests at target SLO** and defends it. An extensible system knows where the **next three changes will land** and isolates them. Cheap cuts spend; frugal cuts waste. Generic everywhere is not extensible — it is just slow and expensive to run.
What frugality actually means

Frugality in HLD is not minimal spend. It is **maximum useful work per dollar, watt, byte transferred, and operator hour, without breaking correctness or SLOs**. Measure it as `cost / successful request` broken down by compute, memory, storage retained, network egress, and third-party calls. If you cannot quote that number and say which component dominates it, you do not have a frugal design — you have hope. The trade-off is explicit: every byte you avoid reading, every hop you avoid taking, every replica you avoid running saves money but removes margin, redundancy, or debuggability. Frugal accepts that trade and prices it.

Extensibility is not plugin frameworks and abstractions everywhere. It is **the cost and blast radius of the next change**. A system is extensible if you can add a new request type, pricing rule, notification channel, or region without editing the hot path, migrating all stored data, or redeploying every service. That requires stable boundaries: a core domain that rarely changes, versioned contracts around it, and explicit extension points where variation is expected. The trade-off is also explicit: each seam you add costs per-request overhead, cognitive load, and test matrix growth. Extensibility pays that tax only where change is probable.
Why they belong together

Interviewers pair them because naive extensibility destroys frugality, and naive frugality destroys extensibility. Make everything generic and configurable and your `p99` climbs, your cache hit rate collapses, and your per-request CPU doubles — you bought future flexibility with present waste on every call. Inline everything for speed and the next product requirement forces a rewrite of storage format, API contract, and deployment — you bought present efficiency with future engineering quarters. The correct posture is **frugal on the hot path, extensible at the edges**: tight, boring, measurable execution for the 95% of traffic that never changes, plus narrow, versioned seams where product, scale, or regulation will force change.
The mechanism: budgets on the hot path, seams off it

You implement frugality with **budgets and accounting**, not intentions. Every request gets a resource budget: time, downstream calls, bytes scanned, egress. You enforce it with quotas, deadlines, pagination, compression, caching, and shedding. You implement extensibility with **stable interfaces and isolation**: versioned APIs, event schemas with backward-compatible evolution, policy or strategy interfaces for volatile rules, and async side-effects so new consumers do not block core flow. The trade-off that governs both: enforcement and indirection cost CPU and latency now to avoid cost explosions and rewrites later. Put the enforcement where waste actually happens and the indirection where change actually happens — anywhere else is overhead without return.

blocks.title: Frugal request path
blocks.caption: Every request passes quota, deadline, and cost accounting; expensive work is cached, bounded, or shed.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  R[Client request] --> G[Gateway auth quota deadline]
  G --> C[App logic with budget]
  C --> K[Cache lookup]
  K --> D[Bounded read]
  D --> S[Storage]
  C --> M[Cost meter]
  M --> Q[Quota shed or degrade]

blocks.text: This path is deliberately stingy. The gateway rejects unauthenticated, over-quota, or oversized work before it burns downstream resources — why pay for work you will discard? App logic carries a deadline and a fan-out limit, so one slow dependency cannot multiply cost across retries. Cache sits before storage because network and disk reads dominate most bills. The cost meter is not observability decoration; it attributes CPU, bytes scanned, and egress per endpoint and tenant so you know what to optimize next. Trade-off: quotas and deadlines create user-visible rejections and partial results. That is the price of protecting shared resources. Without them, one tenant or feature pays for itself with everyone else's budget.

blocks.title: Extensible seams
blocks.caption: Core stays stable; variation lives behind versioned interfaces and async events.
blocks.code:
graph LR
  Core[Core domain] --> API[Versioned interface]
  API --> P1[Rule plugin A]
  API --> P2[Rule plugin B]
  API --> E[Domain events]
  E --> N1[New consumer 1]
  E --> N2[New consumer 2]

blocks.text: This seam layout is deliberately narrow. The core owns invariants — money movement, ordering, access control — and changes slowly. Volatile logic such as pricing, fraud checks, or routing lives behind a `Policy` interface with explicit versioning, so adding a rule does not fork the hot path. State changes emit versioned events, so new readers like analytics, notifications, or a second region subscribe without modifying writers. Trade-off: versioned contracts and events add serialization cost, storage for multiple schema versions, and eventual consistency for consumers. You pay latency and complexity at the boundary to avoid coupling and big-bang migrations in the core.
Trade-offs, honestly on both sides

blocks.caption: Each efficiency or flexibility wins somewhere and loses somewhere else.
rows: Far fewer reads, lower p99 and storage-read bill
Invalidation bugs, stale reads, extra write fan-out and storage
Lowest latency and CPU per request, simple trace
Any new variant edits core; deploys and rollbacks couple all features
New types added without core change
Per-call dispatch, harder profiling, combinatorial test matrix
Writers stay frugal; new consumers attach freely
Eventual consistency, duplicate delivery, schema-version debt
Noisy neighbors, quota and isolation machinery, correlated failure
Low utilization; you pay for idle capacity on every tenant

blocks.text: The pattern is that frugality pushes you toward **sharing, batching, and cutting hops**, which increases blast radius and staleness risk. Extensibility pushes you toward **isolation, versioning, and async boundaries**, which increases per-request cost and operational surface. Name that tension in the interview. Say: *I will share the hot read pool across tenants for utilization, and I will accept quota and bulkheading work to contain it. I will isolate volatile rules behind an interface, and I will accept 1-2ms dispatch plus contract tests to carry it.* If you cannot state the price, you did not make a decision.
How it fails in production

Frugality fails as **slow cost bleed, then sudden cliff**. Symptoms: cost per 1k requests drifts up 2% per deploy while latency looks fine, cache hit rate decays after a new query pattern, retry storms multiply downstream calls 3-5x during partial outages, or retained storage grows unbounded because no TTL or compaction was priced. You see it in the bill before the dashboard: egress or scan volume spikes, idle replicas at 8% CPU at 3am, or one endpoint consuming 70% of database read units. The cause is almost always unbounded work — no pagination limit, no deadline, no fan-out cap, no backpressure. Fix is budgets: cap page size, enforce timeouts with hedging only where measured, add quota per tenant and per key, and make the cost meter alert on unit cost, not just total spend.

Extensibility fails as **abstraction collapse or version paralysis**. Symptoms: adding a field requires a coordinated deploy of four services, plugin ordering becomes load-bearing and undocumented, v1/v2/v3 handlers all run in production because no one can deprecate, or event consumers silently diverge because schema evolution was additive in name only. You see it in lead time: a one-line rule change takes two weeks, or a rollback rolls back unrelated features because they share a deployable. The cause is seams in the wrong place — generic where behavior is stable, hardcoded where it varies — plus missing ownership of contracts. Fix is fewer, better seams: one versioned interface per axis of change, contract tests owned by the producer, sunset policy with dates, and synchronous validation at the edge with async propagation inside.

items: Bill climbs while traffic is flat — unit cost regression, not growth.
`p99` fine but `p99.9` explodes — unbounded fan-out orScan under deadline.
Cache hit rate drops after launch — new access pattern bypasses key design.
Retry + timeout amplification — caller retries faster than callee recovers.
Schema v1-v4 all live — no deprecation owner, test matrix explodes.

blocks.text: What good looks like in config and code

This snippet carries both ideas in twelve lines. The `RequestBudget` makes frugality enforceable: page caps, call caps, byte caps, and a deadline are parameters, not comments. Rejecting oversized work early is cheaper than executing it and discarding the result — trade-off is a stricter API that some clients will dislike. The `Policy` plus `Registry` makes extensibility bounded: new behavior means registering `(name, version)`, not branching core code. Version pinning lets old and new coexist during rollout — trade-off is you must own deprecation or versions accumulate forever. In review, point at the meter you omitted here: every `decide()` should emit `calls, bytes_scanned, cpu_ms` by `(policy, version)` so unit cost per extension is visible.
How this shows up in the interview

items.title: Force the unit economics first
items.text: Ask what dominates cost: ingress, compute, storage retained, or egress? Then state target unit: cost per 1k writes, per active tenant, per GB retained per month. Without that, every optimization is theater.

items.title: Draw the hot path and bound it
items.text: Walk one read and one write end to end. Put numbers: cache hit target, page limit, fan-out limit, deadline, retry budget. Say what you shed when the budget is exceeded.

items.title: Name the axes of change
items.text: Ask what will vary in 12 months: new request types, new rules, new regions, new consumers? Place exactly one seam per axis. Refuse generic extensibility anywhere else.

items.title: Version the contracts
items.text: Show API and event evolution: additive fields, default handling, dual-read or dual-write during migration, sunset date. Extensible without a deprecation story is just debt with a nicer name.

items.title: Close with what you would measure
items.text: Unit cost per endpoint and tenant, cache hit rate, bytes scanned per request, version adoption, and time to add a rule without touching core. If those move the right way, the design works.

blocks.text: Misconceptions that fail you

items: Frugal means cheapest infra or fewest services — it means lowest cost per useful result at SLO; underprovisioning that violates SLO is waste, not savings.
Extensible means configurable everything — unbounded flags and plugins raise per-request cost and make behavior untestable.
Caching fixes cost — it trades read cost for invalidation, staleness, and write amplification; measure hit rate by key class.
Async fixes coupling — it trades deploy coupling for consistency and duplicate-delivery handling; idempotency is mandatory.
Serverless or autoscaling automatically saves money — they trade idle cost for per-invocation cost and cold starts; spiky, short work wins, steady hot paths often lose.
One more abstraction future-proofs the design — each seam needs an owner, contract tests, and a sunset plan or it becomes permanent overhead.

blocks.text: When to pay for it and when not to

blocks.caption: Frugality is always measured; extensibility is paid for only where change is likely.
rows: Pays back on every request; invalidation cost is contained
Change is certain; isolation beats repeated core edits
Generic machinery here is pure overhead
Lets readers attach without taxing writers
Unit-cost work here never repays engineering time
Quotas and pagination now, sharding later
Budgets are cheap insurance; premature distribution is expensive irreversibility

blocks.text: The judgment call is sequencing. Budgets, pagination, idempotency, and versioned contracts are cheap on day one and ruinous to retrofit — build them in. Cross-region active-active, fine-grained multi-tenancy, and elaborate rule engines are expensive on day one and straightforward to add behind a seam later — defer them but leave the seam. Trade-off stated plainly: early frugality buys survival, early over-extensibility buys drag. Instrument unit cost from the start so the moment a shortcut stops paying, the data tells you before the bill does.

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: Say: **I will bound every hot path with explicit budgets to hold unit cost at SLO, and isolate likely change behind one versioned seam per axis — frugal by default, extensible where change pays.**
